title: How we made the first comprehensive map of deaths along the US border’s “virtual wall”
gist: MIT Technology Review describes how it built the first comprehensive map of migrant deaths near US Customs and Border Protection surveillance towers, merging nearly 4,000 death records from No More Deaths, Humane Borders and 14 Texas county sheriffs with the Electronic Frontier Foundation's catalog of roughly 600 towers, then dating tower installations from satellite imagery and running a topographical viewshed analysis. The methodology exposes how little of this data the US government itself collects or publishes.

insights.claim: Border Patrol estimates more than 10,000 people have died crossing the US-Mexico border since 2000, a figure widely considered an undercount because there is no national protocol for how records of recovered remains are handled.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: When the responsible agency cannot count its own outcome variable, third-party datasets become the only basis for evaluating a multibillion-dollar program.
insights.quote: The US-Mexico border has been called the world’s deadliest land border
insights.locator: The US-Mexico border has been called the world’s deadliest land border

insights.claim: Texas was the biggest missing link in existing migrant-death databases because, unlike Arizona, it has no initiative to share records online and, unlike New Mexico, it leaves death investigations to individual counties.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Data availability is a function of state administrative design, so geographic gaps in any border dataset are structural rather than random.
insights.locator: Public records requests in Texas

insights.claim: Records requests to Texas justices of the peace can stall for years and sometimes omit scene details entirely, because some justices never visit the scene and instead formally declare a person dead over FaceTime with first responders.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Illustrates how thin the evidentiary chain is behind official border-death statistics that policy and procurement decisions rest on.
insights.quote: some justices never even visit the place where a migrant died, instead formally declaring the person deceased over FaceTime with the first responders on scene
insights.locator: In most of these counties, locally elected administrative judges

insights.claim: Most sheriff and county agencies do not record whether a dead person is believed to have been crossing the border, even though Zapata County reports include a checkbox for whether jewels were stolen in a burglary and Cameron County reports one for whether a burglar entered through a chimney.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: A vivid test of institutional priorities: the categories an agency chooses to digitize reveal what it actually intends to measure.
insights.quote: Zapata County reports have a checkbox to indicate whether jewels were stolen in a burglary, for example, while Cameron County reports have one for whether a burglar entered through a chimney
insights.locator: Those delays were compounded because most agencies do not record

insights.claim: Obtaining county death records required near-daily calls, cost between $300 and $1,300 per county in some cases, and one county's per-record fee was cost prohibitive, leaving usable records from 14 of 17 targeted Texas counties.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Quantifies the friction cost of public-records journalism and why comparable datasets do not exist commercially.
insights.locator: After we filed a request, it took periods of near daily calls

insights.claim: The final analysis pooled more than 1,500 cases from Texas sheriff records, more than 1,700 from Humane Borders (sourced from Arizona's Pima County medical examiner), and nearly 1,000 from No More Deaths, for a total of nearly 4,000 cases with location precise enough to use.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
entities: Pima County Office of the Medical Examiner
insights.so_what: The denominator for every downstream claim about deaths near towers — anyone contesting the findings has to contest this pool first.
insights.locator: Total cases reviewed

insights.claim: Anthropic's Claude, accessed via API, was used to extract coordinates from case reports for the three counties that sent the largest volumes of records, with batches then verified by hand for accuracy.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Concrete evidence of LLMs entering investigative document pipelines as extraction infrastructure with human spot-checking, a growing enterprise use case.
insights.quote: we used Anthropic’s Claude, accessed via API, to inspect each case report and pull out coordinates of the spots where remains were found; then we checked batches of those cases by hand to verify the AI’s accuracy
insights.locator: Except for the reports from Kenedy, Webb, and Hidalgo Counties

insights.claim: Only cases with GPS coordinates precise to within 300 feet (Humane Borders) or a quarter-mile (No More Deaths) were included, and several hundred cases were dropped for insufficient location detail — a deliberately conservative screen that biases the resulting death count downward.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Conservative inclusion rules mean the headline death totals should be read as a floor, which matters when the agency's rebuttal is that the numbers are inflated.
insights.locator: Humane Borders notes for each case how precise the location description is

insights.claim: Government records suggest about 800 surveillance towers are currently deployed while the Electronic Frontier Foundation has logged only about 600, so any independent analysis systematically misses deaths near towers that have not been catalogued.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: A quarter of the installed base is effectively invisible to outside oversight — the gap between deployed and catalogued assets is where accountability disappears.
insights.quote: government records suggest that about 800 towers are currently deployed, while EFF has logged about 600
insights.locator: The Electronic Frontier Foundation has been tracking and mapping CBP surveillance towers since 2023

insights.claim: Installation dates had to be reconstructed from multiple satellite imagery sources because no public record exists; Anduril towers are comparatively easy to date since they appear on previously empty desert with trademark solar panels, while integrated fixed towers were often built on existing structures.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Shows that commercial satellite imagery is now a workable audit tool for physical infrastructure deployments that vendors and agencies do not disclose.
insights.locator: This is easier for certain tower types than others

insights.claim: Satellite imagery can establish only that a tower was present, not that it was powered, functional or transmitting, so presence-based analyses cannot distinguish a working sensor network from a field of inoperative hardware.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: The central caveat to all tower-effectiveness claims in either direction — uptime data remains the missing variable in evaluating the program.
insights.quote: Our analysis therefore establishes when a tower was present, not whether it was operational.
insights.locator: Another limitation is that even if a tower is visible at a particular time

insights.claim: Multiple Border Patrol agents said that even towers marketed as mobile, such as autonomous towers, are in practice very rarely taken down or moved, a claim corroborated by semipermanent fences erected around many Anduril tower sites.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Undercuts the flexible-redeployment selling point of mobile surveillance systems: in the field they behave like fixed infrastructure.
insights.locator: But most tower systems are permanent structures

insights.claim: A death counted as being in range only if it fell within the tower's published surveillance range and the tower was already present during the estimated death window, with any case whose window began before the tower's first appearance excluded outright.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: The two-criteria screen is the methodological core critics will attack; it is deliberately asymmetric toward exclusion.
insights.locator: But for a given match between a set of remains and a tower to count

insights.claim: Where records gave no death estimate, skeletal remains were conservatively assumed to have lain at least six months, and a three-year rule was applied — a case counted only if the tower had stood for at least three years before the remains were found.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Explains why the published counts are floors: dozens of ambiguous cases were discarded rather than assigned.
insights.locator: Many cases involve skeletal remains

insights.claim: Published tower ranges are advertised estimates rather than contractual guarantees, and some government records redact site-specific surveillance range information citing security concerns.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Vendor range specifications are marketing numbers that buyers apparently do not lock into contracts — a red flag when sizing capability claims.
insights.quote: But they are advertised estimates, not contractual guarantees
insights.locator: To know how far the main tower types could see

insights.claim: Viewshed analysis drew a sight line between each tower's estimated height and an assumed 5-foot-6 person, using elevation data where each grid square covers 30 meters and carries a single elevation value, so fine terrain variation in rugged areas is lost.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: The line-of-sight findings are directional estimates, not simulations of what a camera saw — useful for aggregate patterns, weak for any single case.
insights.locator: Viewshed

insights.claim: Vegetation is treated as a minor obstruction because virtual-wall towers use thermal imaging that detects body heat through light brush, while buildings could not be modeled at all and urban-area towers were simply flagged as caveats.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Thermal capability is why the it-was-hidden-by-brush defense is weak for these systems, narrowing the range of innocent explanations for missed detections.
insights.locator: It’s much harder to estimate whether a line of sight was blocked by vegetation

insights.claim: Border Patrol does not disclose which alerts came in around any given migrant death, and tower footage is not retained unless an internal investigation is triggered — which happens only if a migrant dies in custody.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Retention policy structurally prevents after-the-fact accountability, so external estimates will remain the only evidence base until retention rules change.
insights.quote: footage isn’t retained unless an internal investigation is triggered, which doesn’t happen unless a migrant dies while in custody
insights.locator: This is all but impossible to answer with records or data

insights.claim: Dozens of interviews with former Border Patrol, CBP and DHS staff and presidential advisors surfaced instances where surveillance technology underperformed and underscored how seldom its effectiveness is evaluated internally.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Procurement continues without an internal efficacy feedback loop — the condition under which vendor revenue is most durable and least tied to performance.
insights.locator: MIT Technology Review instead conducted dozens of interviews

insights.claim: A media request to visit the expanding Anduril tower deployment in Big Bend, Texas was approved at the local Border Patrol level in July 2026 but denied when it reached DHS headquarters for final sign-off.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Headquarters-level information control tightening around the newest tower deployments signals sensitivity about their performance.
insights.locator: Beginning in September 2025, MIT Technology Review requested interviews

insights.claim: Of the contractors sent detailed questions before publication, CBP and Anduril responded without substantively addressing them, General Dynamics deferred to CBP, and Elbit did not respond at all.
insights.speaker: James O'Donnell
insights.so_what: Uniform non-engagement across three prime contractors suggests coordinated reputational risk management around tower efficacy questions.
insights.locator: Before publishing our investigation, we sent detailed questions
